title: Europe’s Dangerous Hesitation on Its Own Air Defense
gist: Even a US license to build Patriots would not fix Ukraine's air defense: America makes a little over 600 PAC-3 interceptors a year while Ukraine alone burns 150-180 in a single intensive month, and Washington now refuses to share seeker, solid-rocket-motor and guidance technology. The argued fix is deterrence by counter-force - a NATO that credibly threatens to 'shoot the archer' rather than only intercept.

insights.claim: The United States produces a little more than 600 PAC-3 interceptors annually and aims to triple that output in coming years, while Ukraine alone can expend 150 to 180 interceptors in a single month of intensive Russian attacks.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Interceptor demand exceeds supply by roughly an order of magnitude in one theater alone - a multi-year structural backlog for missile-defense primes and their solid-rocket-motor and seeker suppliers.
insights.quote: The United States produces a little more than 600 PAC-3 interceptors annually; the goal is to triple that number in the coming years.
insights.locator: It would take years to build new production facilities

insights.claim: Licensing Patriot interceptor production to Ukraine would not solve its air defense problem because new production facilities take years to build, so the binding constraint is industrial capacity rather than legal permission.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Policy headlines about licensing or tech transfer are noise; watch facility groundbreakings, solid rocket motor capacity and seeker lines for the real supply signal.
insights.locator: It would take years to build new production facilities

insights.claim: Ukraine's cities cannot be protected from Russian ballistic missiles under current inventories, regardless of which political requests Washington grants.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Implies continued Russian strike leverage over Ukrainian infrastructure and a persistent risk premium on Ukrainian reconstruction and energy assets.
insights.quote: There are simply not enough interceptors to protect its cities from Russian ballistic missiles.
insights.locator: But even if these things were to happen

insights.claim: Trump has backed away from hints that he might grant Ukraine a license to build Patriot interceptors, and Washington has apparently declined Kyiv's request for 300 such interceptors.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence the US is rationing scarce air-defense output for its own magazines rather than allied demand - a bullish structural signal for interceptor order books, bearish for Ukrainian defensive coverage.
insights.locator: U.S. President Donald Trump has now backed away

insights.claim: The Trump administration appears unwilling to transfer sensitive interceptor technologies - seekers, solid rocket motors and guidance software - to Ukraine, keeping the highest-value parts of the missile stack inside US industry.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: The choke points in missile defense are seekers, SRMs and guidance software; firms holding those capabilities retain pricing power and are not being diluted by offshore licensing.
insights.quote: the Trump administration now seems to be unwilling to share sensitive interceptor technology, including seekers, solid rocket motors, and guidance software, with the Ukrainians
insights.locator: It would take years to build new production facilities

insights.claim: A NATO that credibly signals it will strike the launchers and their operators - not merely intercept incoming missiles - would strengthen deterrence and prevent war in the first place.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Argues European defense budgets should tilt from pure interceptor stockpiles toward long-range strike, ISR and suppression capabilities - a different procurement basket than air defense alone.
insights.quote: A NATO that credibly signals that it will not only attempt to defend against incoming missiles but also shoot the archer would strengthen deterrence, preventing war in the first place.

insights.claim: Roughly 80 percent of the interceptors for a key US missile defense system have been depleted, according to sources cited in accompanying CNAS coverage.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: A depleted magazine forces either urgent multi-year replenishment contracts or reduced US forward presence - both are tradeable, and the former favors munitions suppliers.
insights.quote: Sources: 80% of Interceptors for Key Missile Defense System Depleted

insights.claim: The gap between US interceptor inventories and requirements is described as generational, meaning it cannot be closed quickly and has major implications for US military power globally.
insights.speaker: CNAS
insights.so_what: Frames munitions scarcity as a decade-long theme rather than a one-off supplemental - supports sustained defense-industrial capex exposure.
insights.quote: This is a generational gap that cannot be overcome in a short amount of time, and that has major implications for U.S. military power and security around the globe.
